name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q01 - Structural identification of sarcomere functional bands

questiontext.text:
The diagram given below represents the anatomical organisation of a relaxed myofibril sarcomere:

Identify the myofibril landmarks labelled P, Q, R, and S:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The provided schematic illustrates a single sarcomere of a striated muscle fibre bounded between lateral structural boundaries. Four specific anatomical regions are indicated: a dark vertical boundary line denoted by P, the region containing solely thin filaments denoted by Q, the dark central region spanning the total length of thick filaments denoted by R, and the central non-overlapped segment of thick filaments denoted by S.

Step 2: Assumptions and Biological Principles
Under the sliding filament model of skeletal muscle, myofibrils exhibit alternate isotropic (light) and anisotropic (dark) bands created by the regular overlap of thin (actin) and thick (myosin) myofilaments. The fundamental structural and contractile unit extending from one transverse Z disc to the next is defined as a sarcomere.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Scientific Definitions
- Z line: The elastic fibrous line running perpendicularly through the centre of each I band to anchor thin filaments.
- I band (Isotropic band): The light zone comprising only thin actin filaments.
- A band (Anisotropic band): The dark zone spanning the full length of the thick myosin filaments, including regions of actin-myosin overlap.
- H zone: The central portion of the A band that is not overlapped by thin actin filaments during the relaxed resting state.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Interpretation of Labels
- Structural line P marks the boundary elastic membrane that bisects the light band, confirming that P is the Z line.
- Region Q spans the zone between the Z line and the outer lateral boundary of the thick filaments, encompassing only thin filaments; therefore, Q represents the I band.
- Region R marks the entire longitudinal span of the thick filaments, establishing that R is the A band.
- Region S denotes the central gap between the opposing free ends of the thin filaments, establishing that S is the H zone.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying spatial order and histological correspondence demonstrates complete agreement: P is the Z line, Q is the I band, R is the A band, and S is the H zone. Therefore, the correct identification links P with Z line, Q with I band, R with A band, and S with H zone.

answer.text: P - Z line, Q - I band, R - A band, S - H zone
P - M line, Q - A band, R - I band, S - H zone
P - Z line, Q - H zone, R - A band, S - I band
P - M line, Q - I band, R - H zone, S - A band

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q02 - Biochemical domains of meromyosin monomer molecule

questiontext.text:
The diagram given below illustrates the structural domains of a single meromyosin monomer from a myosin thick filament:

Select the option that correctly identifies the labelled domains P, Q, R, and S:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram displays the macromolecular structure of a meromyosin molecule, the subunit of a myosin thick filament. Distinct sub-structures are marked: an apical binding site designated as P, a subapical binding site designated as Q, the projecting outward segment comprising the head and neck designated as R, and the elongated basal filamentous shaft designated as S.

Step 2: Assumptions and Biological Principles
Thick filaments are polymers of individual meromyosin proteins. Each meromyosin monomer is functionally cleaved into two segments: heavy meromyosin (HMM) and light meromyosin (LMM). The globular head contains enzymatic and mechanical binding machinery, while the tail aggregates to form the structural shaft of the thick filament.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Scientific Definitions
- Heavy Meromyosin (HMM): Comprises the globular head and short arm, forming the cross arm that projects outward from the filament surface.
- Actin-binding site: Located at the tip of the globular head to engage thin filaments during cross-bridge formation.
- ATP-binding site: Located on the globular head possessing active ATPase enzymatic activity to hydrolyze ATP.
- Light Meromyosin (LMM): The elongated helical rod-like tail portion of the meromyosin monomer.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Interpretation of Labels
- Label P points to the apical interaction zone on the globular head where contact with the F-actin filament is established; thus, P is the actin-binding site.
- Label Q identifies the catalytic pocket where ATP binds and undergoes enzymatic hydrolysis; thus, Q is the ATP-binding site.
- Bracket R encompasses both the dual globular heads and the flexible short neck, which project outward as the cross arm (heavy meromyosin component); thus, R represents the cross arm.
- Bracket S encloses the elongated coiled-coil tail portion constituting light meromyosin; thus, S represents the tail.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying each domain confirms that P is the actin-binding site, Q is the ATP-binding site, R is the cross arm, and S is the tail. Therefore, the correct identification links P with actin-binding site, Q with ATP-binding site, R with cross arm, and S with tail.

answer.text: P - ATP-binding site, Q - Actin-binding site, R - Tail, S - Cross arm
P - Actin-binding site, Q - ATP-binding site, R - Cross arm, S - Tail
P - Actin-binding site, Q - Calcium-binding site, R - Light meromyosin, S - Heavy meromyosin
P - Troponin-binding site, Q - ATP-binding site, R - Cross arm, S - Light meromyosin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q03 - Macromolecular organization of thin contractile filament

questiontext.text:
The diagram below depicts the macromolecular architecture of a thin (actin) filament in skeletal muscle:

Which of the following options correctly identifies the protein components P, Q, and R?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram illustrates the molecular anatomy of the thin contractile myofilament found in striated myofibrils. Three biochemical constituents are demarcated: periodic trimeric globular complexes labelled P, two long continuous fibrous strands labelled Q, and two intertwined chains of spherical protein beads labelled R.

Step 2: Assumptions and Biological Principles
The thin filament is a multi-protein assembly composed of three proteins: actin, tropomyosin, and troponin. Actin forms the structural backbone, while tropomyosin and troponin regulate myosin binding in a calcium-dependent manner.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Scientific Definitions
- F-actin (Filamentous actin): A double-stranded helix constructed from polymerised spherical G-actin (globular actin) monomers.
- Tropomyosin: Two continuous fibrous protein filaments running along the grooves of the F-actin helix throughout its length.
- Troponin: A complex heterotrimeric protein distributed at regular intervals along the tropomyosin strands that physically blocks myosin-binding sites in the absence of calcium.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Interpretation of Labels
- Label P points to the discrete trimeric globular protein clusters positioned at periodic intervals on the tropomyosin strand; thus, P represents troponin.
- Label Q identifies the elongated fibrous cords running alongside the grooves of the actin polymers; thus, Q represents tropomyosin.
- Label R identifies the double-stranded helical polymer built from spherical monomeric units; thus, R represents F-actin.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying each biochemical identification confirms that P corresponds to troponin, Q corresponds to tropomyosin, and R corresponds to F-actin. Therefore, the correct identification links P with troponin, Q with tropomyosin, and R with F-actin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q04 - Anatomical classification of human thoracic ribs

questiontext.text:
The diagram below provides a schematic representation of the human thoracic cage and rib articulations:

Identify the skeletal categories and elements designated by P, Q, R, and S:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram illustrates the anterior and anterolateral architecture of the human rib cage. Four groups or skeletal entities are highlighted: rib pairs spanning levels 1 to 7 bracketed as P, rib pairs spanning levels 8 to 10 bracketed as Q, the two lowermost rib pairs with unattached anterior extremities bracketed as R, and the flat ventral midline bone indicated by S.

Step 2: Assumptions and Biological Principles
The human thorax comprises 12 pairs of bicephalic ribs that connect dorsally with the 12 thoracic vertebrae. Anatomically and functionally, these ribs are classified into three distinct categories based on their mode of anterior/ventral termination: true ribs, vertebrochondral (false) ribs, and floating ribs.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Scientific Definitions
- True ribs (Vertebrosternal ribs): The first 7 pairs of ribs that attach dorsally to the thoracic vertebrae and connect ventrally directly to the sternum through hyaline costal cartilage.
- Vertebrochondral ribs (False ribs): The 8th, 9th, and 10th pairs of ribs that do not articulate directly with the sternum, but instead join the costal cartilage of the 7th rib.
- Floating ribs (Vertebral ribs): The 11th and 12th pairs of ribs whose anterior tips remain free without any sternal or cartilaginous attachment.
- Sternum: The flat elongated bone positioned along the ventral midline of the thorax.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Interpretation of Labels
- Group P encompasses the first 7 pairs of ribs attaching directly to the sternum, establishing that P represents true ribs.
- Group Q encompasses rib pairs 8, 9, and 10 which merge into the 7th costal cartilage, establishing that Q represents vertebrochondral (false) ribs.
- Group R designates rib pairs 11 and 12 which lack ventral attachments, establishing that R represents floating ribs.
- Indicator S points to the flat ventral breastbone, establishing that S represents the sternum.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking anatomical counts and connection patterns confirms that P represents true ribs, Q represents false ribs, R represents floating ribs, and S represents the sternum. Therefore, the correct identification links P with True ribs, Q with False ribs, R with Floating ribs, and S with Sternum.

answer.text: P - False ribs, Q - True ribs, R - Floating ribs, S - Clavicle
P - True ribs, Q - Floating ribs, R - False ribs, S - Sternum
P - False ribs, Q - Floating ribs, R - True ribs, S - Scapula
P - True ribs, Q - False ribs, R - Floating ribs, S - Sternum
